```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5)
library(BayesianQDM)
```

This vignette describes the analysis of a proof-of-concept (PoC) study with
one normally distributed endpoint. `vignette("overview")` introduces the
decision criteria.

## Model

In group $k$ ($k = t, c$), the outcomes follow $N(\mu_k, \sigma_k^2)$, and
the data are summarized by the number of subjects $n_k$, the sample mean
$\bar y_k$ and the sample standard deviation $s_k$ (`data_continuous()`).
The treatment effect is $\theta = \mu_t - \mu_c$.

With the Normal-Inverse-chi-squared prior (`prior_nix()`),
$$\mu_k \mid \sigma_k^2 \sim N(\mu_0, \sigma_k^2 / \kappa_0), \qquad
\sigma_k^2 \sim \textrm{Inv-}\chi^2(\nu_0, \sigma_0^2),$$
the posterior distribution has the same form with parameters
$\kappa_n = \kappa_0 + n$, $\mu_n = (\kappa_0 \mu_0 + n \bar y) / \kappa_n$,
$\nu_n = \nu_0 + n$ and
$\nu_n \sigma_n^2 = \nu_0 \sigma_0^2 + (n - 1) s^2 +
\kappa_0 n (\bar y - \mu_0)^2 / \kappa_n$, and the posterior distribution of
the mean is the t distribution $t_{\nu_n}(\mu_n, \sigma_n^2 / \kappa_n)$.
With the vague prior $p(\mu, \sigma^2) \propto \sigma^{-2}$
(`prior_vague()`), it is $t_{n - 1}(\bar y, s^2 / n)$.

For the predictive criterion, the mean of $m$ future subjects of a group has
the posterior predictive distribution
$$t_{\nu_n}\left(\mu_n, \; \sigma_n^2 \left(\frac{1}{\kappa_n} +
\frac{1}{m}\right)\right).$$
Version 0.1.0 of the package used the squared scale
$\sigma_n^2 (1 + 1 / \kappa_n) / m$, which treats the $m$ future subjects as
independent draws from the predictive distribution of one subject and
understates the uncertainty.

The posterior and predictive probabilities of the Go and NoGo regions are
probabilities of the difference of two t variables, computed by `ptdiff()`
with one of three methods (argument `method` of `design_continuous()`):

- `"NI"` (the default): numerical integration over the whole real line,
  exact up to a small numerical error;
- `"MM"`: the moment-matching approximation of the difference by a single t
  distribution (Yamaguchi, Homma, Takeda and Maruo, submitted), which
  requires more than 4
  degrees of freedom in both groups;
- `"MC"`: Monte Carlo simulation with `nMC` draws.

## Decision for observed data

A study with 12 subjects in each group and vague priors, with
$\theta_{TV} = 15$ and $\theta_{MAV} = 5$:

```{r design}
crit <- criterion_posterior(theta_tv = 15, theta_mav = 5,
                            gamma_go = 0.6, gamma_nogo = 0.7)
des <- design_continuous(n_t = 12, n_c = 12, prior_t = prior_vague(),
                         prior_c = prior_vague(), criterion = crit)
dec <- qdm_decide(des, data_t = data_continuous(n = 12, mean = 22, sd = 25),
                  data_c = data_continuous(n = 12, mean = 2, sd = 25))
dec
```

The posterior distribution of each mean is $t_{11}(\bar y, s^2 / 12)$. The
three methods of `ptdiff()` give similar probabilities of the Go region:

```{r methods}
post_t <- dec$posterior_t
post_c <- dec$posterior_c
scale_t <- post_t[["sigma"]] / sqrt(post_t[["kappa"]])
scale_c <- post_c[["sigma"]] / sqrt(post_c[["kappa"]])
set.seed(1)
sapply(c("NI", "MM", "MC"), function(m) {
  ptdiff(15, mu_t = post_t[["mu"]], scale_t = scale_t, df_t = post_t[["nu"]],
         mu_c = post_c[["mu"]], scale_c = scale_c, df_c = post_c[["nu"]],
         method = m, lower.tail = FALSE)
})
```

## Prior distributions and external data

An informative Normal-Inverse-chi-squared prior is given by its parameters;
for example, a control prior centered at 0 with the weight of 2 subjects for
the mean and 4 degrees of freedom for the variance:

```{r nix}
des_nix <- design_continuous(
  n_t = 12, n_c = 12, prior_t = prior_vague(),
  prior_c = prior_nix(mu0 = 0, kappa0 = 2, nu0 = 4, sigma0 = 25),
  criterion = crit
)
qdm_decide(des_nix, data_t = data_continuous(12, 22, 25),
           data_c = data_continuous(12, 2, 25))$posterior_c
```

External data enter through a power prior with weight $a_0$: data with $n_e$
subjects, mean $\bar y_e$ and standard deviation $s_e$ act as $a_0 n_e$
subjects with the same mean and the sum of squares
$a_0 (n_e - 1) s_e^2$, which keeps the posterior distribution in closed form
(Huang et al., submitted). With the vague prior, the posterior distribution
of the mean then has $a_0 n_e + n - 1$ degrees of freedom. Borrowing half of
30 external control subjects:

```{r external}
des_ext <- design_continuous(
  n_t = 12, n_c = 12, prior_t = prior_vague(), prior_c = prior_vague(),
  criterion = crit,
  external_c = borrow(data_continuous(n = 30, mean = 0, sd = 25), a0 = 0.5)
)
dec_ext <- qdm_decide(des_ext, data_t = data_continuous(12, 22, 25),
                      data_c = data_continuous(12, 2, 25))
dec_ext$posterior_c
```

The control mean now has `r dec_ext$posterior_c[["nu"]]` degrees of freedom
($0.5 \times 30 + 12 - 1$), and the probability of the Go region is
`r format(dec_ext$prob_go, digits = 3)` (without the external data,
`r format(dec$prob_go, digits = 3)`).

## Hypothetical control

For an uncontrolled study, Kang, Yamaguchi and Han (2026, Section 4.2.4)
give the control mean the same t distribution as the posterior distribution
of the treatment mean, with location $\mu_{0c}$ and the squared scale
multiplied by $r$:
$$\mu_c \sim t_{\nu_{nt}}(\mu_{0c}, \; r \sigma_{nt}^2 / \kappa_{nt}).$$
The prior of the control group is then not used and is left `NULL`:

```{r hypothetical}
des_hyp <- design_continuous(
  n_t = 12, n_c = 0, prior_t = prior_vague(), criterion = crit,
  hypothetical_c = hypothetical(mean = 0, r = 1)
)
qdm_decide(des_hyp, data_t = data_continuous(12, 22, 25))
```

## Fixed control

With `fixed_c`, the control mean is a known value $\mu_{c0}$, for example
the mean of the standard of care reported in the literature. The effect is
$\theta = \mu_t - \mu_{c0}$, its probabilities are those of the t
distribution of the treatment mean, and `prior_c` and `method` are not
used. With the vague prior and a benchmark of $-10$:

```{r fixed}
des_fix <- design_continuous(n_t = 12, n_c = 0, prior_t = prior_vague(),
                             criterion = crit, fixed_c = -10)
dec_fix <- qdm_decide(des_fix, data_t = data_continuous(12, 22, 25))
dec_fix
pt((22 - (-10 + 15)) / (25 / sqrt(12)), df = 11)
```

For the predictive criterion, the mean of the $m_t$ future subjects has the
predictive t distribution given above, and the future effect is that mean
minus $\mu_{c0}$.

## Predictive criterion

With 50 subjects per group in a future study and $\theta_{NULL} = 0$:

```{r predictive}
des_pred <- design_continuous(
  n_t = 12, n_c = 12, prior_t = prior_vague(), prior_c = prior_vague(),
  criterion = criterion_predictive(theta_null = 0, m_t = 50,
                                   gamma_go = 0.9, gamma_nogo = 0.7)
)
qdm_decide(des_pred, data_t = data_continuous(12, 22, 25),
           data_c = data_continuous(12, 2, 25))
```

## Operating characteristics

`qdm_oc()` simulates `nsim` studies under each scenario. Only the sufficient
statistics are simulated, $\bar y = \mu + \sigma Z / \sqrt{n}$ and
$s = \sigma \sqrt{X / (n - 1)}$ with $Z \sim N(0, 1)$ and
$X \sim \chi^2_{n - 1}$, and the same random numbers are used for all
scenarios. The moment-matching approximation is much faster than numerical
integration and is convenient for exploring designs:

```{r oc}
des_mm <- design_continuous(n_t = 12, n_c = 12, prior_t = prior_vague(),
                            prior_c = prior_vague(), criterion = crit,
                            method = "MM")
scen <- data.frame(mu_t = seq(0, 40, by = 5), sd_t = 25, mu_c = 0, sd_c = 25)
oc <- qdm_oc(des_mm, scen, seed = 1)
oc
plot(oc)
```

The chosen design can be checked with numerical integration. To keep this
vignette quick, only three scenarios and 1000 simulated studies are used
here; with the same seed, both methods are applied to the same simulated
studies:

```{r oc-ni}
scen3 <- scen[c(1, 3, 5), ]
oc_ni <- qdm_oc(des, scen3, nsim = 1000, seed = 1)
oc_mm <- qdm_oc(des_mm, scen3, nsim = 1000, seed = 1)
data.frame(mu_t = scen3$mu_t, Go_NI = oc_ni$Go, Go_MM = oc_mm$Go,
           NoGo_NI = oc_ni$NoGo, NoGo_MM = oc_mm$NoGo)
```

The simulation standard error of the probabilities is at most
$0.5 / \sqrt{nsim}$, `r format(0.5 / sqrt(10000), digits = 2)` for the
default `nsim = 10000`.

## Decision boundary

`qdm_boundary()` gives the decision on a grid of observed treatment means
and standard deviations (or sample sizes), and its plot shows which data
lead to Go, NoGo and Gray decisions. With a concurrent control group, the
observed control data are given by `data_c`, and the vertical axis is the
observed difference in means:

```{r boundary}
b <- qdm_boundary(des_mm, mean_t = seq(-10, 50, by = 1),
                  sd_t = seq(10, 40, by = 1),
                  data_c = data_continuous(12, 2, 25))
plot(b)
```

A larger standard deviation needs a larger observed difference for a Go
decision. For the design with a fixed control, the boundary can be drawn
against the sample size instead:

```{r boundary-fixed}
plot(qdm_boundary(des_fix, n_t = 6:40, mean_t = seq(-10, 40, by = 0.5),
                  sd_t = 25))
```

## Calibration of the thresholds

The thresholds are calibrated so that the Go criterion is met with
probability at most 0.05 when the treatment has no effect, and the NoGo
criterion with probability at most 0.2 when the effect is 20:

```{r calibrate}
cal <- qdm_calibrate(
  des_mm,
  scenario_go = data.frame(mu_t = 0, sd_t = 25, mu_c = 0, sd_c = 25),
  scenario_nogo = data.frame(mu_t = 20, sd_t = 25, mu_c = 0, sd_c = 25),
  target_go = 0.05, target_nogo = 0.2, seed = 1
)
cal
plot(cal)
```

The chosen thresholds are $\gamma_{go} =$ `r cal$gamma_go` and
$\gamma_{nogo} =$ `r cal$gamma_nogo`.
